title: Large Language Models, Small Labor Market Effects (revised as: Still Waters, Rapid Currents: Early Labor Market Transformation under Generative AI)
pub: NBER Working Paper 33777 (May 2025, revised March 2026); also circulated as a University of Chicago Becker Friedman Institute (BFI) working paper. Originally titled 'Large Language Models, Small Labor Market Effects'; the March 2026 revision carries the title 'Still Waters, Rapid Currents: Early Labor Market Transformation under Generative AI'.
author: Anders Humlum · Emilie Vestergaard

st.t: AI adoption: Enthusiasm cannot establish investment value
st.an: The source excerpts are survey instruments rather than findings. They measure usage frequency, employer policy, workplace provision and training, which are relevant to the cluster’s organisational framing, but provide no responses or conclusions establishing whether these conditions affect adoption, reliability or investment value.

st.t: Graduate employment: Weakness signals but does not prove displacement
st.an: The excerpts show a registry-based, career-stage comparison of exposed and non-exposed occupations, which is relevant to the cluster’s monitoring framework. However, they provide no readable employment outcomes or causal estimates, so the source’s position on whether early-career weakness signals AI-related displacement cannot be determined.
qs: We follow Brynjolfsson, Chandar and Chen (2025) in defining the age groups: early career 1 (ages 22–25), early career 2 (26–30), developing (31–34), mid-career 1 (35–40), mid-career 2 (41–49), and senior (50+).

st.t: Worker exposure: Technical susceptibility differs from displacement
st.an: The source material is too incomplete to determine whether it accepts, extends or rejects the cluster’s distinction between technical exposure and realised displacement. Truncated tables without interpretable headings or substantive narrative do not support a source-level position.

st.t: Young workers: Automation differs from augmentation effects
st.an: The source is relevant because it separates early-career age groups and compares employment trends in exposed versus non-exposed occupations. However, the supplied excerpt provides no readable trend estimates and does not distinguish automation from augmentation, so it cannot establish whether it supports or challenges the cluster’s proposition.
qs: We follow Brynjolfsson, Chandar and Chen (2025) in defining the age groups: early career 1 (ages 22–25), early career 2 (26–30), developing (31–34), mid-career 1 (35–40), mid-career 2 (41–49), and senior (50+).

st.t: Assisted inequality: Productivity gains need not improve careers
st.an: The source accepts and materially strengthens the cluster’s distinction between assisted productivity, work transformation and labour-market rewards. Its linked Danish evidence finds task reorganisation and reported productivity gains alongside precise null average effects on earnings, wages and recorded hours, while showing that actual chatbot adoption does not explain the observed early-career employment decline. It does not establish long-run career or inequality effects.
qs: These null results hold even among workers who use chatbots daily, report substantial productivity gains, perform new AI-related tasks, or work in firms that encourage and invest in chatbots.

The task creation evidence in Section 2.3 provides a key part of the answer: employers are absorbing generative AI through task reorganization—creating new roles, reassigning responsibilities, investing in training and oversight—rather than adjusting on the margin of total labor input.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s reconfiguration-over-replacement framing and materially strengthens it with linked survey and administrative evidence: adoption is associated with new tasks, oversight and time reallocation, while earnings, hours and employment remain broadly unchanged over the first two years. It also reinforces the importance of organisational complements, though it does not directly assess apprenticeship or competence risks.
qs: The task creation evidence in Section 2.3 provides a key part of the answer: employers are absorbing generative AI through task reorganization—creating new roles, reassigning responsibilities, investing in training and oversight—rather than adjusting on the margin of total labor input.

Yet these currents have not broken the surface: using difference-indifferences, we estimate precise null effects on earnings and recorded hours at both the worker and workplace levels, ruling out effects larger than 2% two years after the launch of ChatGPT.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s work-redesign framing and materially extends it with linked Danish survey and administrative evidence: chatbot adoption creates generation, verification, compliance and integration tasks while producing little measurable near-term change in average earnings, hours or employment. It therefore strengthens the distinction between task-level transformation and realised aggregate labour-market effects, while limiting its conclusions to an early period and qualified causal design.
qs: Using difference-in- differences, we estimate precise null effects at both the worker and workplace levels, ruling out effects larger than 2% two years after ChatGPT’s launch.

st.t: Early careers: Comparative design yields no findings
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s principal proposition: the supplied figure fragments contain labels and occupational panels but no recoverable claims or readable data sufficient to establish AI displacement, labour-market effects, or legal staffing consequences.

st.t: Entry routes: Reduced hiring precedes broader displacement
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s qualified proposition by replicating early-career employment declines in AI-exposed occupations, including legal professionals, while finding that firms’ generative-AI adoption did not drive those declines. It therefore reinforces the distinction between narrowing entry routes and established AI-caused displacement.
qs: The plots show that we replicate the declines in early-career jobs in many exposed occupations, including software developers, legal professionals, marketing professionals, IT support specialists,                                                            34 ^Ljournalists, HR professionals, and financial advisors.
Importantly, however, our difference- in-differences analysis in Section 3.4 shows that the declines are not driven by firms adopting Generative AI.

st.t: Impact measurement: Sample balance does not remove attrition
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s methodological framing: it reports observable-balance, response-quality, incentive and administrative-validation checks without treating them as substantive evidence of AI’s labour-market effects. Its comparison of complete and partial respondents addresses potential attrition bias but does not establish equivalence on unobserved traits or eliminate attrition as an interpretive limitation.
qs: Table B.2 shows that our survey respondents resemble our survey populations on observable characteristics.

22 ^L    Table B.3 shows that complete respondents (who form the basis of our main analysis sample) and partial respondents have similar characteristics and give similar responses to the survey (before partial respondents drop out).

st.t: Knowledge work: Task gains do not ensure skill growth
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s central distinction between early changes in work organisation and demonstrated economy-wide productivity or displacement effects. It finds task and occupational reorganisation despite stable wages and hours, and qualifies entry-level displacement claims by showing that the examined employment declines were not driven by firms that had actually adopted chatbots.
qs: Even as wages and recorded hours remain stable, workplaces adopt chatbot initiatives, workers take on new AI-related tasks, and adopters transition into new occupations.
Our key contribution is to split these trends by whether firms have actually adopted generative AI, revealing that the declines are not driven by firms adopting AI chatbots.

st.t: Labour evidence: Distinct mechanisms resist one AI effect
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s methodological conclusion that fragmentary tables with missing headings and explanatory context cannot reliably establish a unified AI labour-market effect or justify substantive staffing conclusions. It is more restrictive than the cluster, declining to interpret even the partial numerical patterns that the synthesis cautiously distinguishes.

st.t: Youth employment: Exposure measures require competing tests
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s methodological conclusion: it documents occupation- and age-group comparisons, including early-career cohorts, but the supplied figure fragments contain no readable trends or causal evidence establishing AI-driven entry-level displacement.

kp.k: Linked Danish data capture early chatbot labor-market adjustment
kp.d: Humlum and Vestergaard link adoption surveys conducted in November–December 2023 and 2024 to Danish administrative employment records through December 2024. The latest survey covers approximately 25,000 workers across 7,000 workplaces in 11 highly exposed occupations, including legal professionals; Table B.1 identifies 24,796 linked complete responses for 2024. This is the March 2026 revision, previously titled Large Language Models, Small Labor Market Effects, and is a non-peer-reviewed working paper.
qs: Our latest survey round, conducted in late 2024, includes responses from 25,000 workers across 7,000 workplaces.
NBER working papers are circulated for discussion and comment purposes.

kp.k: Adoption has not measurably changed earnings or recorded hours
kp.d: Difference-in-differences estimates compare adopters and non-adopters before and after ChatGPT’s November 2022 launch. Pooled worker estimates rule out average effects larger than 2% through December 2024; dynamic earnings estimates rule out changes larger than 3%. Null findings persist among daily and early adopters, workers reporting substantial benefits or new tasks, and workplaces combining encouragement, enterprise chatbots and training. Occupation-specific estimates are less precise and should not inherit the pooled 2% bound.
qs: Difference- in-differences estimates for earnings, recorded hours, and wages all center on zero, with confidence intervals ruling out average effects larger than 2%.
Nonetheless, we find no statistically significant effects in any occupation, and point estimates are generally near zero.

kp.k: Higher adopter earnings predate chatbot availability
kp.d: Adopters initially appear to earn approximately 9% more with employer encouragement and 4% more without encouragement. The authors find these differences existed before chatbots became available, rather than representing returns to adoption. They discuss amenities, employer reluctance to reward use, and overstated perceived benefits as possible explanations for unchanged pay; these are hypotheses, not established mechanisms. Null results across different wage-setting systems suggest wage rigidity alone is insufficient.
qs: Adopters appear to earn substantial premia of about 9% for those with employer-encouraged usage and 4% for those without.
However, leveraging the panel dimension of our administrative data reveals that these earnings differentials entirely predate the arrival of AI chatbots.

kp.k: Employer encouragement accompanies stronger adoption and perceived benefits
kp.d: Approximately 43% of employers explicitly encourage chatbot use, 21% allow it and 6% prohibit it. Among encouraging firms, 61% have enterprise solutions, 39% provide training and 29% offer both. Predicted worker adoption rises from approximately 41% ever-use and 7% daily use without initiatives to 93% and 28% with all three initiatives. The authors interpret these relationships descriptively, not as experimentally identified causal effects; initiatives are measured through worker perceptions and checked against coworker reports.
qs: Firms now broadly embrace AI chatbots: about 43% explicitly encourage their use, another 21% allow it, while only about 6% explicitly prohibit it.
Among firms that encourage chatbot use, 61% have an enterprise chatbot solution, 39% provide training, and 29% offer both.
Since our data are collected from workers rather than senior leadership, our estimates reflect employer initiatives as perceived by workers.

kp.k: Reported time savings exceed observed earnings changes
kp.d: Appendix E.3 estimates that adopters save approximately 3% of total work hours, combining categorical self-reports of time savings and usage frequency. Legal professionals report 2.6% total time savings; 78.3% report some time savings, 17.8% more than an hour per day of use, and 54.4% improved quality. These are perceived benefits rather than independently measured productivity. Approximately 85% of time-saving adopters indicate allocating saved time to other tasks; the questionnaire frames this allocation as an expectation.
qs: On average, adopters in our sample report savings of about 3% of their work hours.

kp.k: New work includes generation, oversight and integration
kp.d: Without employer initiatives, approximately 8% of users report entirely new tasks; the introduction reports roughly 17% with active initiatives, while Section 2.3 reports roughly 18%. Reported new AI-related tasks include content generation, checking outputs, ethics and compliance, and workflow integration. The authors report approximately 42% associated with content generation and 35% with quality review and compliance, while describing integration as approximately 26% of all new tasks. Training is especially associated with ethics and compliance responsibilities. These findings concern task content, not measured increases in total employment.
qs: About 42% of new AI-related tasks relate to generating new content, including AI Ideation, AI Content Drafting, and AI Data Insights.

Notably, 35% of new AI-related work is dedicated to AI Quality Review and AI Ethics & Compliance, suggesting that AI adoption shifts workers not only toward content generation but also toward supervisory roles overseeing AI outputs.

kp.k: Legal work gains drafting, verification and governance tasks
kp.d: The legal-professional task examples encompass brainstorming arguments, drafting contracts and briefs, researching and summarizing legal materials, reviewing AI-generated documents for accuracy and compliance, developing organizational usage policies, and safeguarding ethics and confidentiality. The authors also note continuing bans in occupations requiring high factual accuracy, including legal professionals. Legal professionals form one occupational group within the broader study; occupation-specific null labor-market estimates carry wider confidence intervals.
qs: Developing organizational AI usage policies and guidelines
Ensuring AI tools and outputs uphold legal ethics and confidentiality

kp.d: Approximately 4% of non-users report additional workloads attributable to chatbots, especially where employers have adopted initiatives. Among teachers who do not use chatbots, 10% report new AI-related workloads, primarily monitoring and responding to students’ use. The authors interpret these spillovers as workplace transformation extending beyond direct adopters, including human monitoring and validation responsibilities.
qs: AI chatbot workloads extend beyond direct users: Figure 3, Panel (b) shows that 4% of non-users report new workloads resulting from AI chatbots, with effects most pronounced in workplaces that have adopted chatbot initiatives.
New tasks extend even to workers who have never used AI chatbots, signaling broader workplace transformation.

kp.k: Occupational mobility rises among chatbot adopters
kp.d: By December 2024, adopters increase hours in their latest occupation by approximately 4% of a full-time equivalent relative to non-adopters. Associations are strongest in IT support and, to some extent, office clerical work, and stronger among daily users and those reporting large time savings than across employer initiatives. Adopters switching occupations experience 12 percentage points faster earnings growth between November 2022 and December 2024 than other Danish workers employed in both months. The authors acknowledge that chatbots could facilitate transitions or that newcomers could find chatbots especially valuable; the earnings comparison is not an isolated causal return to AI.
qs: By December 2024, adopters have increased their hours in their most recent occupation by about 4% of a full-time equivalent relative to non-adopters.
Adopters who switch occupations see 12 percentage points faster earnings growth between November 2022 and December 2024 relative to other Danish workers employed in both months.

kp.k: Adopting workplaces show no differential entry-level displacement
kp.d: The authors replicate declining employment among workers aged 22–25 in several exposed Danish occupations, including legal professions, but do not find those declines concentrated in chatbot-adopting workplaces. Workplace total-hours estimates rule out effects larger than 2%, and early-career employment-share estimates rule out effects greater than one-third of a percentage point. Their illustrative bound attributes at most approximately 0.14 percentage points of an aggregate decline of about 0.6 percentage points between October 2022 and December 2024 to encouraged adoption. Job creation, destruction, wage bills and incumbent outcomes likewise show no differential changes. These findings concern actual adoption during the observed period, not all possible anticipatory effects or future displacement.
qs: Crucially, Panel (b) shows that the decline in early-career jobs is not driven by firms adopting AI chatbots.

Difference-in-differences estimates show no differential changes in the employment share of early-career workers at adopting workplaces, with estimates precise enough to rule out effects greater than a third of a percentage point.
These workers have not experienced differential changes in hours.

kp.k: Identification depends on comparable trends and limited spillovers
kp.d: The observational design assumes adopters and non-adopters would otherwise follow similar outcome changes. Controls, pre-trend analysis, employer-policy comparisons and coworker-based measures support robustness but do not turn adoption into random assignment. Exact adoption dates are unavailable. Difference-in-differences does not directly identify economy-wide effects shared by non-adopters; the authors use aggregation checks, a calibrated equilibrium model and perceived earnings impacts to argue that these spillovers are small. Survey sampling conditions worker-level analysis on employment in target occupations, so incumbent-worker analyses separately examine displacement.
qs: The key identifying assumption is that, absent AI chatbots, adopters and non-adopters would have experienced similar changes in labor market outcomes.
Our survey does not record the exact timing of adoption, precluding event studies indexed to workers’ month of first use.
Virtually all respondents—97.7% of adopters and 99.5% of non-adopters—state that AI chatbots have had no impact on their labor earnings.

kp.k: Task reorganization may precede conventional labor-market effects
kp.d: The central interpretation is that employers absorb generative AI through new tasks, reassigned responsibilities, training and oversight rather than immediate adjustments to total labor input. The authors relate this to task reinstatement and productivity J-curves, explicitly treating mutually reinforcing stability in earnings and hours and internal task adjustment as a conjecture. Better-paid occupational transitions may provide a future earnings channel, but the observed switchers are too few to move average adopter earnings. The formal model assumes human-deployed chatbots, so it does not establish effects of autonomous AI coworkers.
qs: We conjecture that these two patterns may be mutually reinforcing: when earnings and recorded hours remain stable, workers and workplaces absorb technological change through task reallocation and other unrecorded adjustments, reducing pressure on pay or hours.
First, AI chatbots affect output only when actively deployed by workers, reflecting current technology that depends on direct human prompting.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Humlum and Vestergaard find substantial changes in work tasks but little measurable change in average earnings, recorded hours or workplace employment during the first two years after ChatGPT’s launch.
pts.d: In the March 2026 revision, the authors report pooled difference-in-differences estimates near zero, ruling out average earnings and recorded-hours effects larger than 2%. They find no statistically significant earnings or workplace employment effects in any study occupation, including legal professionals, although occupation-specific confidence intervals are wider. The null earnings findings also hold for daily users, early adopters, workers reporting substantial benefits and workers whose employers combine encouragement with enterprise tools and training. They interpret task reorganization as an important mode of adjustment, rather than treating stable earnings and hours as evidence that work is unchanged. The proposed mechanism that task reallocation absorbs changes and reduces pressure on earnings or hours is explicitly a conjecture.

pts.k: Employer initiatives are associated with higher chatbot adoption and reported benefits, while AI creates new drafting, verification, compliance and integration work.
pts.d: The authors report that adoption peaks where encouragement, enterprise chatbots and training are combined: 93% have used chatbots at work and 28% use them daily. These are descriptive associations rather than experimentally identified effects of employer initiatives. Across occupations, adopters report estimated savings averaging about 3% of work hours; Table E.3 reports 2.6% for legal professionals. Among legal adopters, 78.3% report some time saving, 54.4% improved quality and 17.8% more than an hour saved per day of use. The share reporting entirely new tasks rises from about 8% without employer initiatives to roughly 17–18% with active initiatives. New work includes generating content, checking AI outputs, ensuring compliance and integrating tools. Legal examples include drafting documents, researching and summarizing law, reviewing AI-generated legal analysis, and developing organizational AI policies. The authors also report workloads affecting non-users. Their account of time reallocation is survey-based; the questionnaire asks what workers expect to do if AI saves time.

pts.k: Chatbot adoption is associated with occupational mobility into better-paid, more AI-relevant roles; the authors suggest this could become a channel for broader earnings gains.
pts.d: By December 2024, adopters increased employment in their latest occupation by about 4% of a full-time equivalent relative to non-adopters. This is the paper’s hours-based mobility measure, not a four-percentage-point increase in the probability of switching. Associations are strongest in IT support and, to some extent, office clerical roles. Adopters who switch occupations experience 12 percentage points faster earnings growth between November 2022 and December 2024 than other Danish workers employed in both months. This comparison is descriptive, not an estimate that AI caused a 12-percentage-point earnings gain. The authors acknowledge that chatbots might facilitate transitions or that recent switchers might find chatbots particularly useful. They suggest broader future earnings effects without specifying a date or magnitude.

pts.k: The authors find that actual employer chatbot adoption does not explain observed declines in early-career employment in exposed Danish occupations.
pts.d: The paper replicates declining employment among workers aged 22–25 in several exposed occupations, including legal professions. However, encouraged-use workplaces show no differential decline in their early-career employment share, with confidence intervals ruling out changes exceeding approximately one-third of a percentage point. The authors calculate that the largest decline consistent with these bounds would imply only about a 0.14-percentage-point aggregate reduction, compared with an observed approximately 0.6-percentage-point decline from October 2022 to December 2024. They also find no differential changes in job creation, destruction or incumbent outcomes. They suggest macroeconomic changes or anticipatory hiring freezes as possible explanations, not established causes. This is their Danish adoption-based finding, not a direct causal test of the United States results cited from other researchers.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence combines worker adoption surveys, administrative employment records, descriptive task reports and difference-in-differences analyses.
pts.d: The main 2024 survey covers approximately 25,000 workers across 7,000 workplaces; Table B.1 identifies 24,796 complete responses linked to registers, or 21.6% of invitees. Surveys were conducted in November–December 2023 and 2024. Administrative records supply monthly earnings, hours, occupations and employer–employee links through December 2024. Event studies compare adopters and non-adopters around November 2022, controlling for occupation and predetermined characteristics; pooled specifications include adopter-specific trends. Robustness analyses examine employer policies, coworker reports, firm characteristics, task mixes and adoption intensity. Reported productivity benefits are not independently measured task productivity, and new-task descriptions were classified by two coders. Occupational-switcher earnings comparisons use descriptive regressions. The task-reorganization interpretation draws on these findings and task-based technology theories; the productivity J-curve is an interpretive analogy rather than an observed later productivity upswing. The source is a working paper, not a peer-reviewed publication.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The findings concern Denmark through December 2024, not labor-market outcomes through the March 2026 revision date or the effects of future autonomous AI.
pts.d: The document was first circulated in May 2025 and revised in March 2026, but the outcome window ends in December 2024, roughly two years after ChatGPT’s November 2022 launch. Adoption timing is not recorded precisely, so the event studies use the launch rather than each worker’s adoption month. Identification requires comparable counterfactual changes for adopters and non-adopters. Difference-in-differences cannot directly identify effects shared by comparison groups; the authors assess such spillovers using additional aggregate evidence, perceived impacts and an equilibrium model, concluding they are small under the model’s assumptions. Anticipatory employment changes unrelated to actual adoption could push estimates toward zero. The 2% pooled bounds should not be assigned to each occupation separately. The formal model assumes human-prompted tools. Future broader earnings gains and a productivity J-curve remain possibilities without a specified realization date.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The source concerns workers and workplaces in 11 AI-exposed Danish occupations, including legal professionals, rather than law firms or legal markets alone.
pts.d: The sample includes accountants, customer support specialists, financial advisors, HR professionals, IT support specialists, journalists, legal professionals, marketing professionals, office clerks, software developers and teachers. Effects are examined for adopters, non-adopters, early-career workers, incumbents and employers with different adoption initiatives. Legal workers report drafting, research, verification, confidentiality and governance tasks; the paper also identifies persistent restrictions on use where factual accuracy is important. Table C.1 reports that 56.1% of the legal-professional sample works in the public sector, so this is not solely private-practice evidence. Table B.5 labels the corresponding legal category 'Paralegals', whereas most of the paper uses 'Legal Professionals'; the source does not support treating the entire group as licensed lawyers. It does not separately estimate effects for law-firm partners, associates, in-house legal departments, ALSPs, client fees or access to justice. Occupational mobility benefits are most evident outside licensed occupations, particularly in IT support and clerical work.
